title: Infectious Gastrointestinal Diseases
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)

overview.intro: This chapter covers infection along the whole digestive tract: the mouth and teeth, the esophagus, the small and large bowel, and the liver. The organisms differ, but the reasoning is the same each time. Ask what normally keeps the organism in check, which cell or layer it attacks, and whether it damages tissue by invasion, by toxin, or through the host immune response. That mechanism predicts the stool (watery or bloody), the lesion (plaque, vesicle, ulcer, or abscess), the timing, and the complication. Board questions give a setting, such as recent antibiotics, a cruise ship, an AIDS patient with painful swallowing, or a serology panel, and ask you to name the organism and predict what comes next.

Intestinal fluid secretion through CFTR and absorption through sodium-coupled transport

blocks.text: The healthy colon holds a dense anaerobic flora that resists colonization by newcomers. Part of that resistance is metabolic: resident bacteria convert primary bile acids into secondary bile acids, and they use up the nutrients a newcomer would need. Primary bile acids such as taurocholate trigger germination of C. difficile spores, while secondary bile acids inhibit growth of the vegetative cells.

Clostridioides difficile is a gram-positive, spore-forming, obligately anaerobic bacillus. Its spores survive drying, alcohol hand rubs, and many surface disinfectants, so they persist on hospital surfaces and hands and are swallowed. Almost any antibiotic can disturb the flora, but clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, and cephalosporins carry the highest risk. Older age, hospital or nursing home stay, and acid suppression add risk, and disease can follow even a single dose or begin weeks after the drug is stopped.

blocks.title: From antibiotic exposure to pseudomembranes
steps: Antibiotic depletes resident colonic flora
Secondary bile acids fall; primary bile acids rise
Ingested spores germinate into toxin-producing cells
Toxins A and B glucosylate Rho family GTPases
Actin collapses, tight junctions open, colonocytes die
Neutrophils, fibrin, and mucus form pseudomembranes
blocks.caption: Loss of colonization resistance lets spores germinate; toxin injury and the neutrophil response build the pseudomembranes.

blocks.text: The organism does not invade. Disease is caused by two large exotoxins. Toxin A (TcdA) is mainly an enterotoxin that draws fluid and neutrophils, and toxin B (TcdB) is a more potent cytotoxin. Both enter colonocytes and glucosylate Rho, Rac, and Cdc42, the GTPases that maintain the actin cytoskeleton. The cells round up, tight junctions open, fluid leaks into the lumen, and dying cells release IL-8 and other signals that recruit neutrophils. Some epidemic strains also make a binary toxin and produce more toxin A and B.

Grossly the colon shows raised yellow-white plaques scattered over a reddened mucosa. Microscopically the exudate bursts out of damaged crypts in a mushroom or volcano pattern. Patients have watery, usually nonbloody diarrhea, cramping, fever, and often a marked neutrophil leukocytosis. In severe colitis the inflamed wall loses tone and the colon dilates (toxic megacolon, usually a transverse colon diameter over about 6 cm with systemic toxicity), which can perforate.

Diagnosis rests on finding the toxin or its genes in unformed stool, by enzyme immunoassay for toxin or by nucleic acid amplification for the toxin B gene. Because people can carry the organism without disease, a positive test is meaningful only in a patient with three or more unformed stools in a day. Endoscopic pseudomembranes are characteristic but not required.

blocks.predict: Why does a patient develop C. difficile colitis after a course of antibiotics even though the antibiotic did not bring the organism?
blocks.explain: The antibiotic removed the resident flora that made secondary bile acids and competed for nutrients, so swallowed spores could germinate and the toxin-producing cells could multiply.
blocks.check: Compare with the first paragraph and the flow figure on colonization resistance.

blocks.text: Diarrhea becomes bloody when the organism breaks the mucosa, either by invading epithelial cells or by killing them with a cytotoxin. The result is dysentery: frequent small stools with blood, mucus, and pus, cramping, and tenesmus. Invasive bacteria usually cause fever and many fecal leukocytes. Two useful exceptions are EHEC, which is not invasive and usually causes little or no fever, and Entamoeba histolytica, whose trophozoites lyse neutrophils so fecal leukocytes may be scant.

blocks.text: Hemolytic uremic syndrome after EHEC

Shiga toxin has one A subunit and five B subunits. The B subunits bind the glycolipid Gb3, which is abundant on glomerular endothelium. The A subunit removes an adenine from the 28S ribosomal RNA of the 60S subunit, halting protein synthesis and injuring the endothelial cell. Hemolytic uremic syndrome follows in roughly 5 to 15% of infected children, about 5 to 10 days after diarrhea begins.

blocks.title: Shiga toxin to hemolytic uremic syndrome
steps: EHEC in colon releases Shiga toxin
Toxin absorbed and binds Gb3 on renal endothelium
A subunit inactivates 60S ribosome; endothelium injured
Platelet microthrombi form in glomerular capillaries
Red cells sheared into schistocytes; platelets consumed
Anemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury
blocks.caption: Endothelial injury, not bacterial invasion, explains each part of the HUS triad.

blocks.text: Postinfectious immune complications

Guillain-Barre syndrome follows Campylobacter infection in a small fraction of cases, usually 1 to 3 weeks later, and Campylobacter is the most commonly identified antecedent infection. The lipooligosaccharide of some strains mimics peripheral nerve gangliosides such as GM1, so antibodies raised against the bacterium bind the axolemma or myelin and cause an ascending, areflexic, flaccid weakness.

Reactive arthritis is a sterile, asymmetric oligoarthritis of the lower limbs that appears 1 to 4 weeks after infection with Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, or Yersinia (or after Chlamydia urethritis). It may come with conjunctivitis and urethritis and is strongly associated with HLA-B27, which is thought to shape how bacterial antigens are presented and how long they persist in the joint.

blocks.predict: A child has bloody diarrhea without fever after a barbecue. A week later the urine output falls and the platelet count is low. What links the two events?
blocks.explain: EHEC releases Shiga toxin that binds Gb3 on glomerular endothelium; endothelial injury causes microthrombi, red cell fragmentation, platelet consumption, and renal failure.
blocks.check: Compare with the Shiga toxin flow figure.

sections.title: Infectious esophagitis in the immunocompromised patient

blocks.text: The esophagus is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium over a lamina propria that holds capillaries and fibroblasts. Intact epithelium, saliva, and peristalsis normally keep organisms from establishing infection. When T cell immunity fails, as in HIV infection with low CD4 counts, transplantation, chemotherapy, or high-dose corticosteroids, three agents dominate: Candida, herpes simplex virus (mostly HSV-1), and cytomegalovirus. All three cause odynophagia, which signals mucosal ulceration, and dysphagia.

Each organism produces a different lesion because it infects a different cell. Candida grows on and into the squamous surface. HSV infects squamous epithelial cells, so its damage is in the epithelium and its inclusions are found in the squamous cells at the edge of an ulcer. CMV does not infect squamous cells well; it infects endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and macrophages in the lamina propria, so its ulcers form by injury to the tissue beneath the epithelium and its inclusions lie in the ulcer base. This is why a biopsy for HSV is taken from the ulcer edge and a biopsy for CMV from the ulcer base.

Most common type; in HIV usually CD4 below about 100 per microliter

blocks.caption: The cell each organism infects predicts the lesion, the inclusion, and where the diagnostic tissue lies.

blocks.text: Candida is the most common cause and often coexists with oral thrush, but thrush can be absent. Esophageal candidiasis, and CMV disease outside the liver, spleen, and nodes, are AIDS-defining conditions. HSV and CMV ulcers may coexist with Candida, so finding plaques does not exclude a viral cause in a patient with severe odynophagia. Pill injury and reflux esophagitis are the main noninfectious alternatives.

The watery diarrhea of these infections arises in the small intestine, which handles most of the fluid entering the gut each day. It occurs when absorption by the villus enterocytes is lost or when crypt secretion is switched on. Neither process requires killing many cells or invading the mucosa, so the stool is large in volume and free of blood and neutrophils. The main danger is loss of water, sodium, potassium, and bicarbonate, causing dehydration, hypokalemia, and a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis.

blocks.text: Cholera is the model of secretory diarrhea. The toxin's B subunits bind GM1 ganglioside on enterocytes, and the A1 fragment ADP-ribosylates the alpha subunit of Gs. This blocks its GTPase activity, so adenylyl cyclase stays on. ETEC heat-labile toxin works the same way; ETEC heat-stable toxin reaches the same result through guanylate cyclase C and cGMP.

blocks.title: How cholera toxin produces rice-water stool
steps: B subunits bind GM1 on enterocytes
A1 fragment ADP-ribosylates Gs alpha
Gs cannot hydrolyze GTP; adenylyl cyclase stays active
cAMP rises; protein kinase A opens CFTR
Crypt cells secrete Cl-; Na+ and water follow
Villus NaCl absorption is also inhibited
blocks.caption: Secretion is switched on without cell death, so the stool is watery, clear, and free of blood and pus.

blocks.text: Sodium-glucose cotransport through SGLT1 remains intact in cholera, which is the physiologic basis for glucose-sodium oral rehydration. Incubation time follows mechanism. A preformed toxin in food, as with emetic B. cereus or Staphylococcus aureus, causes vomiting within hours because nothing needs to grow. Organisms that must colonize and then make toxin, such as ETEC and V. cholerae, take a day or more.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading the timing
blocks.text: Twelve people at a buffet develop vomiting about 3 hours after eating fried rice that was cooked the day before and kept warm. Step 1: onset in hours means a preformed toxin; an infection that must multiply could not act this fast. Step 2: vomiting dominates, which fits an emetic toxin acting on the gut and vagal afferents. Step 3: rice that sat warm lets B. cereus spores, which survive boiling, germinate and make cereulide, which reheating does not destroy. Compare a passenger who develops diarrhea and vomiting 36 hours after boarding a ship along with many others: a delay of 1 to 2 days and person-to-person spread fit norovirus.

sections.title: Plaque, periodontal disease, caries, and tooth abscess

blocks.text: The periodontium anchors each tooth. The gingiva seals around the neck of the tooth through junctional epithelium, leaving a shallow sulcus about 1 to 3 mm deep. Below it, collagen fibers of the periodontal ligament run from cementum on the root to the alveolar bone of the jaw. Within minutes of cleaning, salivary glycoproteins coat the enamel as a pellicle, and bacteria attach to it and build dental plaque, a biofilm whose matrix protects them from saliva and host defenses.
Gingivitis and periodontitis

Plaque left at the gum line for days to weeks provokes gingivitis: red, swollen gums that bleed on brushing. The inflammation is confined to the gingiva and the attachment is intact, so removing plaque returns the tissue to normal. As plaque matures below the gum line, the flora shifts toward gram-negative anaerobes, including Porphyromonas gingivalis. P. gingivalis makes proteases called gingipains that degrade host proteins and disrupt complement, and it alters the local immune response so that inflammation increases while the bacteria survive.

Most of the tissue loss in periodontitis is done by the host. Neutrophils, macrophages, and lymphocytes release IL-1, TNF, prostaglandin E2, and matrix metalloproteinases that digest ligament collagen, and RANKL from activated T cells and stromal cells drives osteoclasts to resorb alveolar bone. The junctional epithelium migrates down the root and the sulcus deepens into a periodontal pocket. Ligament and bone do not regrow on their own, so the attachment loss is permanent and teeth become mobile and are lost. Smoking and poorly controlled diabetes are the main systemic risk factors.
Dental caries and tooth abscess

Streptococcus mutans uses glucosyltransferases to turn dietary sucrose into sticky glucans that anchor it within plaque, and it ferments sugars to lactic acid while tolerating the acid it makes. When plaque pH falls below about 5.5, enamel hydroxyapatite dissolves. Saliva buffers acid with bicarbonate and supplies calcium and phosphate for remineralization, and fluoride is built into enamel as fluorapatite, which resists acid. Caries results when acid attacks outpace repair, so frequent sugar intake and low saliva flow raise risk.

blocks.title: From sugar to periapical abscess
steps: S. mutans ferments sucrose to lactic acid
Plaque pH below about 5.5 dissolves enamel

Bacteria reach the pulp; pulpitis develops
Pulp swells in a rigid chamber and necroses
Infection exits the root apex: periapical abscess
blocks.caption: Caries becomes an abscess when infection passes through the dead pulp and out of the root tip into bone.

blocks.text: The pulp is enclosed in a rigid chamber, so inflammatory swelling compresses its vessels and the pulp dies. Infection then leaves through the root apex into the surrounding bone. When no sinus tract drains the pus, pressure builds, and the tooth throbs and is very tender to biting or tapping. A periapical abscess differs from a periodontal abscess, which forms in a periodontal pocket beside a living tooth. Untreated dental infection can spread into the fascial spaces of the face and neck; infection from lower molars can reach the submandibular space; bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces is Ludwig angina.

Candida albicans lives harmlessly in the mouth of many healthy people. Several defenses keep it in that state: resident bacteria compete for space and nutrients, saliva flushes the surface and carries antimicrobial proteins, the epithelium sheds and renews, and Th17 cells release IL-17 and IL-22 that recruit neutrophils and stimulate antifungal peptides from epithelial cells. CD4 T cell immunity therefore guards the mucosa, while neutrophils guard against spread into the blood and deep organs.

Thrush, or pseudomembranous candidiasis, is overgrowth on the oral mucosa when one of these defenses fails. It appears as creamy white, curd-like plaques on the buccal mucosa, tongue, palate, or pharynx. The plaques are made of yeast, pseudohyphae, desquamated epithelium, and debris, so they scrape off and leave a red, sometimes bleeding base. A potassium hydroxide preparation or Gram stain shows budding yeast with pseudohyphae. In tissue, Candida forms pseudohyphae and true hyphae, which help it adhere and penetrate.

blocks.title: Who gets thrush and why
rows: Immature T cell immunity and a resident flora not yet established; Candida may be acquired during vaginal birth
Drug deposited in the oropharynx suppresses local immune responses
Glucose in saliva feeds the yeast; hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil function
Loss of CD4 T cells and Th17 responses; thrush is common once CD4 falls below about 200 to 300 per microliter
Dentures, dry mouth, chemotherapy, and systemic corticosteroids
blocks.caption: Each risk factor removes competition, mucosal immunity, or neutrophil function.

blocks.text: Thrush in a healthy adult with none of these risks suggests undiagnosed immunodeficiency, especially HIV. Thrush that extends into the esophagus with pain on swallowing means more severe immunosuppression. Two white lesions must be told apart. Oral hairy leukoplakia, caused by Epstein-Barr virus, forms white corrugated patches on the lateral tongue that do not scrape off. Leukoplakia, a white patch from epithelial thickening that can be premalignant, also does not scrape off.

sections.title: Stomatitis: vesicles and ulcers of the mouth

blocks.text: Stomatitis means inflammation of the oral mucosa. Most painful oral lesions are either vesicles that rupture into ulcers, which suggests a virus, or ulcers that begin as ulcers, which suggests aphthae. The site in the mouth, the age of the patient, fever, and lesions elsewhere on the body sort the causes.

Primary herpes simplex virus type 1 infection in young children often causes herpetic gingivostomatitis. HSV-1 is an enveloped double-stranded DNA virus that replicates in mucosal epithelial cells, causing them to swell, fuse into multinucleated giant cells, and separate into vesicles. Fever, irritability, and tender cervical nodes accompany swollen, red, bleeding gums and clusters of vesicles on the gingiva, tongue, buccal mucosa, and lips that break into painful ulcers. The virus then travels up sensory axons and becomes latent in the trigeminal ganglion. Reactivation produces herpes labialis at the lip border, not a repeat of the widespread primary illness.

Coxsackie A viruses are nonenveloped positive-sense RNA enteroviruses that spread by the fecal-oral and respiratory routes, mostly in summer and fall. In herpangina, fever and sore throat come with small vesicles and ulcers on the posterior mouth: the soft palate, uvula, and tonsillar pillars, while the gums are spared. In hand-foot-and-mouth disease, usually from coxsackie A16 (enterovirus 71 and coxsackie A6 also cause it), oral ulcers on the tongue and buccal mucosa come with vesicles on the palms, soles, and often the buttocks.

Aphthous ulcers (canker sores) are not infections. They are shallow, round, painful ulcers with a gray-yellow fibrin base and a red rim, appear on nonkeratinized mucosa such as the inner lips, cheeks, and floor of the mouth, have no vesicle stage, and recur. They are thought to reflect T cell-mediated injury to the epithelium. Recurrent aphthae can signal systemic disease: Crohn disease, which can involve any part of the gut from mouth to anus; Behcet disease, a vasculitis with recurrent oral and genital ulcers and uveitis that is linked to HLA-B51; celiac disease; and deficiency of iron, folate, or vitamin B12.

Vesicles and ulcers on soft palate, uvula, tonsillar pillars; gums spared

Vesicles on palms, soles, and buttocks
Round ulcers with fibrin base and red rim on nonkeratinized mucosa; no vesicles
Crohn disease, Behcet disease (genital ulcers, uveitis), celiac disease, nutrient deficiency
blocks.caption: Location within the mouth, a vesicle stage, and lesions on the hands, feet, or genitals separate the four.

blocks.predict: A 3-year-old has fever and painful ulcers. Where in the mouth would you expect them if the cause is coxsackie A herpangina rather than primary HSV-1?
blocks.explain: Herpangina affects the posterior mouth (soft palate, uvula, tonsillar pillars) and spares the gums; primary HSV-1 involves the gingiva and the front of the mouth and lips.

blocks.text: Hepatitis B virus is an enveloped, partially double-stranded DNA virus (Hepadnaviridae) that copies its genome through an RNA intermediate using its own reverse transcriptase. Each marker in a serology panel comes from a specific part of the virus or of the immune response, so knowing the source of each marker makes the panel readable without memorizing patterns.

blocks.title: What each hepatitis B marker means
rows: Surface (envelope) protein, made in great excess
Acute or recent infection; the only marker in the window period
Past or ongoing infection; never produced by vaccination
Secreted protein from the precore and core gene
blocks.caption: Core antigen itself stays inside the virion and infected cells, so serum tests detect antibody to core, not core antigen.

blocks.title: Markers over time in acute hepatitis B that resolves

HBeAg and HBV DNA rise; patient highly infectious
Symptoms and ALT rise; IgM anti-HBc appears
HBeAg falls and anti-HBe appears
HBsAg clears, usually by 4 to 6 months
Window: IgM anti-HBc alone until anti-HBs appears
Recovery: anti-HBs plus lifelong IgG anti-HBc
blocks.caption: Surface antigen and its antibody rarely coexist, which creates the window period between them.

blocks.text: Liver injury in hepatitis B is caused mainly by cytotoxic T cells killing infected hepatocytes, which is why ALT and symptoms rise with the immune response rather than with the first appearance of virus. The window period exists because anti-HBs forms immune complexes with the large amount of HBsAg in serum, so free antibody becomes detectable only after the antigen has cleared. A patient tested in that gap is HBsAg negative and anti-HBs negative and could be wrongly called uninfected unless anti-HBc is measured.

blocks.title: Reading a hepatitis B panel
blocks.caption: Anti-HBc separates infection from vaccination, IgM versus IgG separates recent from old, and HBsAg beyond 6 months defines chronic infection.

blocks.text: Chronic carriers may be HBeAg positive, with high viral DNA and high infectivity, or HBeAg negative with anti-HBe. HBeAg-negative carriers can still have active disease when precore mutant virus replicates without making HBeAg, so HBV DNA is the better guide to replication. An isolated IgG anti-HBc with no HBsAg or anti-HBs usually means a remote infection in which anti-HBs has waned, but it can also reflect low-level occult infection or a false positive result.

blocks.title: Worked example: a hepatitis B panel
blocks.text: A health care worker has HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative, IgM anti-HBc positive, and ALT about 600 U/L (reference about 7 to 56 U/L). Step 1: anti-HBc is positive, so this person has been infected; vaccination alone never produces anti-HBc. Step 2: the antibody is IgM, so the infection is recent. Step 3: HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBs is not yet detectable. This is the window period of an acute infection that is resolving. If the same person instead had HBsAg positive and IgG anti-HBc a year later, the infection would be chronic. If the only positive marker were anti-HBs, the person would be immune from vaccination.

Whether a hepatitis virus is cleared depends on the vigor of the T cell response and on the virus's ability to evade it. A strong response clears virus but causes acute hepatitis; a weak or tolerant response causes little early injury but lets the infection persist. Persistence matters because years of hepatocyte death and regeneration lead to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and cancer.

blocks.text: Age at HBV infection is the strongest predictor of chronicity. A neonate infected at birth, especially from an HBeAg-positive mother, has an immature T cell response, and maternal HBeAg crossing the placenta is thought to induce tolerance. The virus therefore replicates with little liver injury for years, and about 90% of such infants become chronic carriers. Most adults mount a vigorous cytotoxic T cell response, have a clinically obvious acute hepatitis, and clear the virus.

HCV takes the opposite course. Acute infection is usually mild or silent, yet most adults never clear it. Its RNA-dependent RNA polymerase lacks proofreading, so the virus exists as a quasispecies, and variants in the envelope protein E2, especially its hypervariable region, keep escaping neutralizing antibody and T cell recognition.

The two viruses cause cancer by different routes. HBV DNA integrates into the host genome, which can disrupt or activate cellular genes, and its HBx protein interferes with p53 and growth control, so hepatocellular carcinoma can arise in a noncirrhotic liver. HCV is an RNA virus that does not integrate; its cancers arise mainly from chronic inflammation, regeneration, and cirrhosis.

Chronic HCV stimulates B cells continuously, and clonal B cells make an IgM rheumatoid factor that binds polyclonal IgG and viral antigen. These complexes precipitate in the cold (type II mixed cryoglobulinemia) and deposit in small vessels and glomeruli, where they fix complement and cause a type III hypersensitivity vasculitis. The result is palpable purpura of the legs, arthralgia, weakness, peripheral neuropathy, and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, with low C4. HCV is also associated with B cell lymphoma, porphyria cutanea tarda, and lichen planus.

The liver receives blood from the portal vein, which drains the bowel, and from the hepatic artery, and it drains bile through the biliary tree. Each of these channels is also a route for infection. Kupffer cells normally clear the small numbers of gut bacteria that enter portal blood, but a large load, an obstructed bile duct, or impaired host defense allows an abscess to form.

A pyogenic abscess is a cavity of pus made of neutrophils and necrotic liver. The most common route is biliary: stones, strictures, or cancer obstruct the ducts, bile stagnates, and bacteria ascend (ascending cholangitis), often producing several abscesses. Portal spread comes from intra-abdominal infection such as appendicitis or diverticulitis, sometimes with septic thrombophlebitis of the portal vein (pylephlebitis). Arterial spread occurs during bacteremia, as with Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis. Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae are the leading organisms, often with streptococci of the anginosus group and anaerobes. Hypervirulent Klebsiella strains, common in East Asia and in people with diabetes, can cause a single abscess and seed the eye or brain. Patients are usually older adults with fever, right upper quadrant pain, leukocytosis, and a raised alkaline phosphatase.

An amebic abscess follows intestinal infection with Entamoeba histolytica. Trophozoites that have invaded the colon wall enter portal venules and are carried to the liver, most often the right lobe, which receives most of the blood from the cecum and ascending colon. They kill hepatocytes and neutrophils on contact, so the cavity fills with liquefied liver and blood rather than true pus. The aspirate is thick, odorless, and reddish brown (anchovy paste), and trophozoites are found mainly in the abscess wall rather than in the fluid. Patients are typically young men who have lived in or traveled to an endemic area, often months earlier, and many have no current diarrhea. Serum antibody to E. histolytica is usually positive, while stool microscopy is often negative.

integration.text: Microbiology and pathology meet in the mechanism of injury. Organisms that switch on secretion through cAMP or cGMP (V. cholerae, ETEC) cause watery small-bowel diarrhea without inflammation, organisms that invade or kill colonocytes (Shigella, Campylobacter, Salmonella, Entamoeba) cause dysentery, and the host response itself causes much of the damage in periodontitis and hepatitis B. Immunology explains the postinfectious diseases: molecular mimicry in Guillain-Barre syndrome, HLA-B27 in reactive arthritis, and immune complexes in HCV cryoglobulinemia.

Anatomy explains the spread. Portal venous drainage carries amebae and gut bacteria to the liver, rigid tooth and fascial compartments turn dental infection into abscess and deep neck infection, and Gb3 on glomerular endothelium makes the kidney the target of Shiga toxin. The limits of the patterns are real: stool tests detect carriage as well as disease, a negative HBsAg does not exclude acute hepatitis B, and organisms overlap in their presentations, so the setting, timing, and mechanism must be read together.

summary: Antibiotics remove the colonic flora that blocks C. difficile; toxins A and B inactivate Rho GTPases, producing pseudomembranes, watery diarrhea, and risk of toxic megacolon, diagnosed by stool toxin or toxin gene tests.
Bloody diarrhea means invasion or cytotoxic injury: Shigella, Campylobacter, Salmonella, EHEC, and Entamoeba histolytica.
Shiga toxin binds Gb3 on renal endothelium and stops protein synthesis, causing HUS; Campylobacter mimicry of gangliosides causes Guillain-Barre syndrome; HLA-B27 predisposes to reactive arthritis.

In immunocompromised patients, Candida causes white esophageal plaques, HSV punched-out ulcers with squamous inclusions at the edge, and CMV linear ulcers with endothelial and stromal inclusions in the base.

Watery diarrhea follows lost absorption or toxin-driven secretion: rotavirus in infants, norovirus in outbreaks, ETEC in travelers, cholera from water, and preformed B. cereus toxin from reheated rice.

Plaque causes reversible gingivitis; periodontitis is host-mediated destruction of ligament and bone driven by organisms such as P. gingivalis; S. mutans acid causes caries that can end in periapical abscess.
Thrush is Candida overgrowth when flora, saliva, Th17 or CD4 immunity, or neutrophil function fails; its plaques scrape off, unlike hairy leukoplakia.

Primary HSV-1 affects the gums and front of the mouth with fever, herpangina affects the posterior pharynx, hand-foot-and-mouth adds palm and sole vesicles, and aphthae have no vesicle stage and suggest Crohn or Behcet disease.
In HBV serology, HBsAg means infection, anti-HBs means immunity, IgM anti-HBc means recent infection, IgG anti-HBc means infection at any time, and anti-HBs alone means vaccination.

HBV becomes chronic in most neonates but few adults, HCV in most adults; both cause cirrhosis and cancer, and HCV causes mixed cryoglobulinemia; pyogenic abscesses come from biliary or portal spread, amebic abscesses from colonic amebae.

verify: Frequency figures vary between sources and should be checked against the values NABNE expects: HUS after EHEC O157:H7 (quoted from about 5% to 15% in children), chronic HBV by age (about 90% neonates, 25 to 50% young children, under 5% adults), chronic HCV (quoted from about 55% to 85%), and cirrhosis after chronic HCV (about 10 to 20% over 20 to 30 years).
CD4 thresholds for thrush (about 200 to 300 per microliter), Candida esophagitis (about 100), and CMV esophagitis (about 50) are approximate and differ among references.

The C. difficile testing approach (toxin enzyme immunoassay versus toxin gene amplification, alone or in a multistep algorithm) and the toxic megacolon diameter cutoff (about 6 cm) vary between guidelines; confirm the version NABNE uses.

Some sources attribute periodontitis to a broader group of organisms (Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, Treponema denticola, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans) and describe P. gingivalis as a keystone pathogen; this chapter names only P. gingivalis as the objective does.
Confirm whether NABNE uses the name Clostridioides difficile or the older Clostridium difficile.
The incubation ranges for B. cereus emetic (about 1 to 6 hours) and diarrheal (about 8 to 16 hours) forms, and the ALT reference range in the worked example, are approximate.
